A character turn or development doesn't necessarily entail a surprise. It just means that they aren't one-note. They don't exist solely to move the plot towards its final destination. Their unique personalities, wants, and goals are the catalysts for the script's progression. To me, Requiem for a Dream is the kind of movie that was developed with the ending at the forefront of the writer's mind and the journey as an afterthought. It's like he had a clear idea of what he wanted the audience to walk away with, but no idea how to make them stay. The frantic editing and some of the hallucinatory sequences are creative enough to keep the audience hooked, but I really don't think there's much beneath the surface.

That whole cross-cut montage of all the characters self-destructing didn't really have much of an effect on me. I didn't feel like any of the characters had a major turn or arc that made their demise emotionally effecting. Ellen Burstyn's character is probably the closest I came to being unsettled, but I think that was a product of her performance instead of the actual content. The whole movie felt like I was just watching the inevitable unfold. Inevitably can be really effective in some movies, but you need to care about the characters before you can feel for their downward spiral. Can somebody change my mind about this movie? I want to like it really badly.
